title: Under the Flags
passage:
The lime avenues of the older suburbs were planted a century ago, and the pavements beneath them have been losing ground ever since. A mature lime can lift a fifty-kilo flag by several centimetres in a decade – slowly enough that nobody sees it happen, steadily enough that the council’s insurers see little else. In the mid-sized city where what follows took place, compensation for trips over lifted paving costs more each year than the parks department spends on planting. The remedies have hardly changed in two generations, and every one of them points downwards. Crews grind the raised edges level. Root barriers go in around each new pit. Watering tubes are sunk a metre into the ground, on the old theory that roots chase water and can be lured away from the surface. Each measure buys a season or two. The flags keep rising.

Bronwen Askerholt, a soil scientist who has spent six years coring beneath lifted pavements, believes the remedies mistake where the problem lives. Her group lifted the flags along nineteen streets and mapped every root they found. Half a metre down, in ground compacted by machinery when the streets were first made, there was almost nothing alive: the soil was dry, airless, nearly impenetrable, and the watering tubes had made no measurable difference to it. The roots were somewhere else. In the few centimetres directly beneath the stones – where the slab cools after sunset and moisture condenses on its underside, and where air moves freely through the jointing sand – her team found dense mats of fine root, thickening year on year. “Most of the force, we think, is generated within a hand’s width of the stone,” she says. “The slab shades the ground, waters it every clear night and lets it breathe. It builds the very thing that lifts it.”

The engineering answer is the root cell: an open plastic crate, stacked two or three deep beneath a rebuilt pavement and filled with loose loam. The crates, not the soil, carry the weight of the traffic above, so the loam inside is never compacted. Suppliers sell them as room to grow. Askerholt’s reading is narrower and stranger: the cells move the damp, aired horizon down and away from the stones, so that the underside of a slab stops being the best address on the street. Not everyone was persuaded. Osmund Fearnbeck, a geotechnical engineer who spent twenty years assessing tripping claims for insurers, pointed out that celled or not, the flags must still be laid on a bedding course of sand. “That course is watered and aired on exactly the terms she describes,” he wrote in a trade journal. “The roots will cross the crates and settle in the bedding. A celled pit buys time, at four times the price of an ordinary one.”

The city tried it anyway, and tried it carefully. Thirty-one streets were rebuilt on cells; the facing pavements, under the same rows of trees, were relaid in the ordinary way. For seven years both sides have been surveyed every April with a straightedge and a wedge gauge. On twenty-five streets the celled flags have stayed within tolerance while the ordinary sides opposite have been ground level twice and relaid once. One street failed and taught nobody anything: a water main was renewed halfway along it, and the trench was reinstated badly. And on five, the survey found exactly what Fearnbeck had said it would find – mats of fine root in the bedding sand, riding clear over the crates beneath. The five had one thing in common. They had been bedded to an older specification, on coarse sand laid nearly twice as deep as the current rule allows, and the roots had evidently found it worth living in; the thin, stiff beds elsewhere were apparently not worth the climb. Those five have since been relaid on a thin mortar bed drawn up to Fearnbeck’s own specification. Askerholt’s group had thought his worry overdone. The five streets are his, fairly won; the twenty-five are not.

The surveys measure the stones, and only the stones. Askerholt is careful about the difference. “We are reading the flags, not the roots,” she says. “For all we know, the bedding on the good streets is filling with root that has not yet found its strength. The stones are behaving; that is all I will sign my name to.” The oldest celled pavement is now in its eighth year. This April the inspectors walked it as usual, and under the lime outside number fourteen the wedge gauge showed four millimetres, the same figure as the year before. The reading went into the book.
– Sidonie Welbrace

questions.prompt: What are we told about Askerholt’s findings?

options.text: Her cores could not settle where the lifting force was coming from.
She traced most of the lift to fine roots under the stones.
Her digs showed the ground further down was entirely without roots.
Heavy anchoring roots had been cut during earlier repairs to the streets.

questions.rationale: Key B paraphrases the paragraph-2 excavation result and the load-bearing hedged quote: dense mats of fine root in the few centimetres directly beneath the stones, and “most of the force, we think, is generated within a hand’s width of the stone”. ‘She traced’ keeps the finding attributed to Askerholt, so the option does not upgrade her own hedge into narrator fact. A (over-hedge/mis-scope) tempts because the quote is hedged – but ‘could not settle where the force was coming from’ contradicts the mapped result; the hedge is about degree, not location. C is a quantifier upgrade: the deep ground held ‘almost nothing alive’, not ‘entirely without roots’. D is plausible outside knowledge (root severance during repairs is a real arborist worry) that the passage never states.

questions.prompt: What are we told about the five streets where the treatment failed?

options.text: The crates beneath them had given way under the weight of traffic.
A badly relaid water main, not the trees, had disturbed them.
They had nothing obvious in common beyond their age.
They had been laid on a much deeper bed of coarse sand.

questions.rationale: Key D paraphrases the stated common feature: bedded to an older specification, on coarse sand laid nearly twice as deep as the current rule allows. A fabricates a mechanical cause using passage furniture (the crates carry the traffic; nothing buckled – the roots rode over intact crates). B is an actor swap from the adjacent sentence: the water main wrecked ONE other street, expressly separate from the five. C is the cautious-sounding wrong answer – it flatly contradicts ‘The five had one thing in common’; the hedged tone is bait for the pick-the-modest-option heuristic (rule 13: here the key is the confident specific claim).

questions.prompt: What is implied about the streets where the treatment has worked?

options.text: The trial has no direct view of what is happening beneath them.
Their paving has not shifted at all since the work was done.
They will never have to be taken up again.
Their trees are now drawing water from beneath the road instead.

questions.rationale: One-inch inference from paragraph 5: ‘The surveys measure the stones, and only the stones’ plus Askerholt’s ‘We are reading the flags, not the roots’ and her admission that the bedding on the good streets may be filling with root. Together these imply the trial’s evidence for success is surface-only – no one has direct sight of the ground beneath. B is a quantifier upgrade: ‘within tolerance’ and a stable four-millimetre gauge reading are not ‘not shifted at all’. C is a too-far leap into certainty about the future that the passage – and Askerholt explicitly – refuses. D is the folk theory the passage plants in paragraph 1 (roots chase water) precisely to knock down; nothing says the trees now feed under the carriageway.

questions.prompt: What is the writer’s attitude towards Fearnbeck’s objection?

options.text: She agrees with Askerholt that the worry was overdone.
She finds it mostly wrong but right on one point.
She thinks the results bore it out in full.
She sets out the dispute without taking a side of her own.

questions.rationale: The writer’s own verdict sentence – ‘The five streets are his, fairly won; the twenty-five are not’ – grants Fearnbeck the bedding-course point (five streets failed exactly as he predicted, and his mortar-bed specification was adopted) while denying his general verdict that cells merely buy time. B states exactly that partial vindication. A is a role/attribution swap: ‘overdone’ was Askerholt’s group’s earlier view, which the verdict sentence pointedly does not share. C overshoots the polarity – ‘in full’ is the opposite of partial vindication. D is the neutral-reporter misread; a writer who scores the contest five–twenty-five has taken a side.

questions.prompt: What is this text mainly about?

options.text: The rising cost to councils of people tripping over uneven paving.
How one city’s engineers finally beat the tree roots under its pavements.
Why paving rises over tree roots, and how one city’s remedy has fared.
The case for replacing old street trees with smaller species.

questions.rationale: Whole-text gist: the passage is a mechanism story (the slab builds its own lifting layer) plus a trial of a remedy built on that mechanism, with a mixed, still-open result. C names both halves without overclaiming. A promotes the vivid paragraph-1 claims detail to main topic – and distorts it slightly (‘rising’ is not stated). B mentions the remedy but overshoots: ‘finally beat’ contradicts the five failures and the surface-only evidence. D is a title-plausible theme the text never argues; nobody proposes replacing the trees.
